transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-09
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Sofia Liu (Redwood SE), Raj Patel (Aurelia), Maya Chen (Aurelia), Tom Walters (Aurelia), Hannah Ortiz (Aurelia)

---
[00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone, good afternoon. thanks for joining, we're planning to cover artifact delivery, the offline licensing flow, and the gpu driver packaging. we have marco and sofia from engineering to go deep on install and runtime perf.
[00:12] Raj Patel: hi lena, thanks. this is really important for us - healthcare, lots of regs. we want to validate the offline process, and get the drivers installed in our airgapped lab, and run throughput benchmarks.
[00:22] Marco Ruiz: great, yep. i'll try to walk through the steps and call out where we've seen gotchas. i may use KB-dash cache or KV cash interchangeably in speech, sorry, the transcription might show kv cash sometimes.
[00:34] Maya Chen: quick note, our security team needs the install checksums and the offline license hash, and also a way to verify the artifacts without network access.
[00:43] Sofia Liu: good point. we typically provide signed tarballs + sha256 sums and an offline verification utility that runs on the target host. we'll go through the exact files in a sec.

[02:05] Marco Ruiz: first, artifact delivery options: we support secure transfer via pre-signed asset bundles (for customers with an appliance that can pull), physical media (encrypted USB/HDD) delivered via courier, or a staged s3 export for the customer's transfer team. in airgapped setups we prefer physical media with checksums and PGP signing.
[02:30] Tom Walters: for physical media, what's the chain of custody? our compliance needs a manifest.
[02:37] Lena Park: we provide a manifest, signature, and a transfer checklist. there's a custodian acceptance form that we can include in the package and the license agreement references the delivery method.

[04:00] Marco Ruiz: the bundle contains: runtime binaries, model artifacts (if customer opted in to hosted model export), driver bundles (nvidia installers), install scripts, offline license token, and verification tools. each file is signed and we include a manifest.json - note: manifest name sometimes appears mangled in transcriptions as "manfest".

[05:20] Maya Chen: about the offline license, is it time-bound or node-count bound? we need to map to our procurement.
[05:30] Lena Park: typically we issue a node-bound offline license with a start and end date; there are two stages: the legal agreement and then the license issuance via our licensing portal. for airgap we generate a signed license file you drop into the license dir during install.
[06:10] Raj Patel: do you do dongles? HSM? we use an HSM for keys and want to understand compatibility.
[06:20] Marco Ruiz: we can integrate with customer KMS/HSM for key wrapping; for the offline license file we support both raw signed files and wrapped keys that require a KMS decryption step. we'll need the public key cert from your HSM team to sign the license for your environment.

[08:00] Sofia Liu: moving onto GPU drivers — we package driver installers for common stacks: NVIDIA 535.x and 545.x lines, CUDA 12.2/12.3 builds, and a kernel module shim we sometimes need. we also produce a containerized runbook for installs.
[08:25] Tom Walters: we run RHEL 8.8 with custom kernels; any special kernel config to watch?
[08:31] Marco Ruiz: yes, kernel module signing and secure boot can block nvidia modules. please disable secure boot for the pilot or sign the modules with your key. also ensure DKMS is present if you rely on kernel updates. we'll list recommended kernel flags in the install guide.

[10:10] Marco Ruiz: common gotchas: mismatched CUDA libraries leading to runtime failures, driver mismatches with container runtime (nvidia-container-toolkit), and glibc/kernel ABI mismatches. for those we include a small compatibility checker script you run before install.

[12:00] Sofia Liu: on the runtime side: KV cache behavior and batching are the biggest levers for throughput/latency. for on-prem we recommend enabling KV cache persistence when you have repeated sessions and long prefix reuse. note, "KV cache" often transcribed as "K V cash" or "KV cash" in automated transcripts.
[12:30] Maya Chen: how persistent is the cache? does it require shared storage?
[12:40] Marco Ruiz: the cache can be local memory per instance or persisted to a local NVMe-backed file for restarts. in multi-node setups we currently do not replicate KV cache across nodes; we rely on routing for affinity. if you need a replicated cache, that's an advanced config and we can discuss architecture.

[14:05] Marco Ruiz: batching: we support dynamic batching at the runtime layer -- continuous batching that groups tokens across open requests. there are SLO knobs: max_batch_size and max_wait_ms. tradeoff is latency vs throughput.
[14:25] Raj Patel: what's the best initial config for interactive chat with 50ms tail latency target?
[14:33] Marco Ruiz: for 50ms p95 you'll want to keep max_wait_ms low (5-10 ms) and max_batch_size small (4-8) and use more instances. also enable prefix caching for repeated prompts to shave tokens. we'll supply suggested configs based on your model size and the GPU.

[16:00] Sofia Liu: quantization: we support INT8 and mixed-precision quant profiles; many customers use int8-quant for cost savings. caveat: quality regression risk — we provide eval harnesses and can recommend model-specific quant profiles.
[16:22] Tom Walters: do you ship quantized weights if we want them offline?
[16:27] Marco Ruiz: yes, we can include quantized model artifacts, but they are tied to a specific runtime kernel set; if you change drivers/CUDA the kernel selection might differ and you could see performance variance. that's why we lock a recommended stack in the bundle.

[18:10] Raj Patel: can we run a bench before we commit? we want end-to-end numbers with our prompts.
[18:20] Lena Park: absolutely. we recommend a 3-day pilot in your lab. Redwood will ship artifacts and drivers, your team installs in airgap lab, we run a standard bench (throughput, latency, tail p95/p99, and token cost) and compare to the Redwood hosted baseline.

[20:00] Marco Ruiz: bench plan: day 0 install and smoke test; day 1 synthetic throughput with varying batch sizes; day 2 real prompt workloads and KV cache enabled to measure steady-state; we'll capture traces and token-level timing breakdown. we'll want SSH access to a bastion or a log export after the run (we don't need inbound access if you prefer to just send logs).

[22:40] Maya Chen: security: are install scripts safe to run on offline hosts? we vet them extensively but we'd like a deterministic install and ability to audit.
[22:50] Sofia Liu: yes, scripts are idempotent and we provide a SHA256 manifest plus PGP-signed bundle. we also give a verbose install log and a checklist of file-level permissions. if you want post-install auditing we can include an attest binary that verifies checksums and signatures locally.

[25:10] Marco Ruiz: runtime perf details: on a 8x A100 80GB config, with int8 quant and KV cache hot hits, we've measured token throughput improvements up to 2.6x vs fp16 for certain models, but this is model-dependent. for latency-sensitive use cases we may prefer fp16 with aggressive batching config.

[27:00] Tom Walters: any special NIC config? our cluster uses SR-IOV and we care about CPU pinning.
[27:10] Marco Ruiz: SR-IOV is fine; ensure GPU CPUs are isolated and rtprio isn't interfering; also NIC offloads are useful but can affect TCP latencies. we'll provide tuning guide covering CPU pinning, hugepages, and io_uring knobs where applicable.

[30:05] Raj Patel: does Redwood support mixed clusters (some nodes hosted/dedicated and some air-gap)? we want failover back to hosted during peak.
[30:15] Lena Park: yes, smart routing can failover to hosted variants. offline licenses need to allow fallback — we have a policy where when the route goes to hosted we don't count those tokens against the offline commit, but we need to set that in the license and config. procurement usually wants that explicitly documented.

[32:40] Marco Ruiz: installer flow (high-level): unpack -> verify signatures -> install drivers-> install runtime -> install license -> start service -> run smoke tests. if an error occurs we include a rollback script. these steps are spelled out in the runbook.

[35:00] Maya Chen: what about kernel module signing again — can you sign modules for us?
[35:07] Marco Ruiz: we can provide unsigned modules and instructions, or we can sign modules if you provide a public key and we coordinate. signing for secure boot requires your key, so typically customers sign themselves.

[36:40] Sofia Liu: artifact checksum and verification: we'll provide SHA256 sums and PGP signatures. verification steps are: verify pgp signature on manifest, verify sha256 for each tarball, then run the local verifier which checks file-level perms and expected binary hashes.

[38:20] Tom Walters: what about updates? drivers/security fixes mid-deploy?
[38:28] Lena Park: we provide patch bundles and an update runbook. for airgapped customers patches are delivered as delta bundles to reduce transfer size. there's a staged validation we require before installing in prod.

[40:00] Marco Ruiz: example edge case: if customer applies a kernel update that changes ABI, DKMS may rebuild modules differently and you can get miscompiled modules. we recommend staging kernel updates on a canary host first.

[41:45] Raj Patel: licensing questions: if we scale out more nodes during peak, can we add temporary nodes?
[41:55] Lena Park: yes, we support burst licenses - short-term node licenses. procurement needs to approve and we generate a timebound license file. details are in the SOW.

[44:10] Sofia Liu: on measurable SLOs: we'll capture token-level latency, time to first token, and p95/p99. we'll provide Grafana dashboards you can run locally or export as PDFs.

[46:02] Marco Ruiz: one more runtime perf note: KV cache eviction policy matters. by default we use LRU with size caps; if you have many long sessions we recommend bumping the cache size and ensuring enough GPU memory for cache + model. we can share memory budgeting guidelines per model.

[48:20] Maya Chen: would you be able to provide the verification utility source for internal audit?
[48:27] Lena Park: yes, we can provide source under the approved security review NDA. we'll include links in the doc pack.

[50:00] Marco Ruiz: for the bench we will need a sample prompt set and expected throughput targets. do you have an internal workload?

[50:12] Tom Walters: we'll provide a 1000-prompt sample and an expected SLA of p95 < 120ms for short prompts, and baseline throughput of 50 tokens/sec per GPU for generation workloads.

[51:30] Lena Park: thanks, that's helpful. we'll draft the bench config and send you the exact runner and metrics collection scripts.

[53:10] Sofia Liu: logistics: we'll upload the driver bundles to a secure staging s3 and also create physical media. marco will produce checksums and the PGP signatures.

[55:00] Raj Patel: what about telemetry — does Redwood send any outbound telemetry? we prefer no outbound by default.

[55:10] Marco Ruiz: by default in airgapped mode telemetry is off. we offer an opt-in offline logs export where the runtime collects metrics locally and your team can upload sanitized logs to Redwood if you want analysis. nothing outbound unless you enable it.

[57:40] Maya Chen: can we get a copy of the SOC2 reports and network diagram?

[57:50] Lena Park: yes, i'll attach SOC2 and a sanitized network diagram. we'll also include the artifact delivery checklist and the license template.

[59:05] Raj Patel: ok, recap and next steps?
[59:12] Lena Park: recap: 1) Redwood sends offline license docs and driver bundles with checksums (Marco). 2) Aurelia to confirm hardware list and windows for physical transfer (Tom / Maya). 3) Schedule 3-day bench in week of 7/20. 4) Security artifacts (SOC2, runbook) to be shared.
[59:35] Tom Walters: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[59:42] Lena Park: thanks all, we'll follow up in the CRM with the artifacts.
[60:00] (Recording ends)
